pass1.sentence: Most head injuries are minor, but the NHS says some signs, such as being knocked out, seizures or worsening drowsiness, need 999 or A&E.
pass1.note: NHS 999/A&E signs

pass1.sentence: The NHS lists emergency signs after a head injury, including being knocked out and not waking, a seizure, new weakness or numbness, and trouble with balance or speech; these need a 999 call.
pass1.note: NHS page lists these signs for 999

pass1.sentence: Repeated vomiting, growing drowsiness or confusion, memory loss, or a severe or worsening headache are signs for which the NHS and NHS inform point to A&E.
pass1.note: A&E signs listed

pass1.sentence: NICE sets out when a CT head scan is advised in hospital, with separate rules for adults and for children under 16.
pass1.note: NICE NG232 CT rules for adults 16+ and children

pass1.sentence: After a minor injury, NHS leaflets describe rest, an adult nearby to watch for warning signs, and avoiding alcohol, driving and contact sport.
pass1.note: home care summary

pass1.sentence: Headaches, tiredness and poor concentration are common after concussion and often settle, and Headway and NHS inform advise a GP visit if they last for around two weeks or more.
pass1.note: symptoms usually improve; GP if persisting

pass1.sentence: Most head injuries are minor, such as a bump or a bruise on the head.
pass1.note: NHS page title/overview: head injury and concussion

pass1.sentence: Concussion is a type of head injury in which the brain is shaken inside the skull, causing mild damage, according to Headway.
pass1.note: Headway: brain shakes back and forth inside the skull, causing mild damage

pass1.sentence: Being knocked out is not required, and Headway says fewer than one in ten concussions involve loss of consciousness.
pass1.note: Headway: less than 10% involve loss of consciousness

pass1.sentence: Symptoms Headway lists include dizziness, feeling sick, confusion or trouble processing information, sensitivity to light and changes in vision.
pass1.note: Headway symptom list

pass1.sentence: Headway also says symptoms may not show for several hours or even days after the incident.
pass1.note: Headway: may not manifest for hours or days

pass1.sentence: The NHS head injury page lists signs that need a 999 call.
pass1.note: NHS lists 999 signs

pass1.sentence: These include being knocked out and not waking up, being unable to stay awake, and having a seizure.
pass1.note: NHS: knocked out and not woken, cannot stay awake, seizure

pass1.sentence: Other signs are new numbness or weakness, and trouble with walking, balance, speech or understanding.
pass1.note: NHS: numbness/weakness, walking, balance, speech

pass1.sentence: A fall from a height of more than 1 metre or five stairs, a high-speed impact, a dent in the skull, or a head wound with an object in it also appears on the list.
pass1.note: NHS: fall over 1 metre or 5 stairs, high-speed, skull dent, object in wound

pass1.sentence: The NHS adds that a change in behaviour counts as a warning sign.
pass1.note: NHS: change in behaviour

pass1.sentence: The NHS and NHS inform describe A&E for lost consciousness, growing drowsiness or confusion, memory loss, repeated vomiting and a severe or worsening headache.
pass1.note: A&E signs listed

pass1.sentence: Bruising around the eyes or behind the ears is also on the A&E lists.
pass1.note: A&E list includes bruising around eyes/behind ears

pass1.sentence: For milder concerns, such as vomiting or dizziness, or for someone who takes blood-thinning medicine or has a blood-thinning condition, the NHS points to NHS 111.
pass1.note: NHS: NHS 111 route for vomiting, dizziness, blood thinners

pass1.sentence: If getting to A&E safely is not possible, the route is to call 999.
pass1.note: NHS: phone 999 if cannot get there safely

pass1.sentence: In hospital, staff assess the person after a head injury.
pass1.note: NICE NG232 is guidance for assessment and early management

pass1.sentence: NICE guidance, written for health professionals, sets out when a CT head scan is advised.
pass1.note: NICE NG232 recommendations/algorithm

pass1.sentence: For adults aged 16 and over, one main trigger is a lower-than-normal score on a standard alertness scale two hours after the injury.
pass1.note: NICE: GCS below 15 at 2 hours

pass1.sentence: A scan within eight hours is also advised for some people who were knocked out or have memory loss and have certain risk factors, and for some people at higher risk of bleeding, such as those on anticoagulant medicines.
pass1.note: NICE: scan within 8 hours for LOC/amnesia with risk factors; anticoagulants

pass1.sentence: For children under 16 the rules are separate and include suspected non-accidental injury and some dangerous mechanisms of injury.
pass1.note: NICE: children triggers

pass1.sentence: Children with only one of the less serious risk factors are usually observed for a minimum of four hours, with a scan if new risk factors appear.
pass1.note: NICE: observe min 4 hours

pass1.sentence: Most head injuries in young children are minor, but local NHS guidance sets out when to seek emergency care.
pass1.note: NHS inform minor head injury / NHS trust leaflets: most minor

pass1.sentence: Signs described for a 999 call include being hard to wake, a seizure, vision changes, numbness or weakness, trouble walking or speaking, and fluid leaking from the ears or nose.
pass1.note: Child head injury leaflets list these 999 signs

pass1.sentence: A&E is described for a baby under one year old if there is worry, and for older children who were knocked out, keep vomiting, have a headache that painkillers do not ease, or have memory or balance problems.
pass1.note: Child leaflets A&E list

pass1.sentence: A noticeable change in behaviour, such as unusual irritability, is also listed.
pass1.note: Child leaflets: behaviour change

pass1.sentence: Some NHS leaflets say an adult should watch the child for 48 hours, though trusts differ a little.
pass1.note: Leaflet: observe child 48 hours; thresholds differ between trusts

pass1.sentence: For a minor injury sent home after assessment, NHS leaflets describe rest as the main treatment.
pass1.note: Rest is main treatment per NHS leaflets

pass1.sentence: They describe an adult staying with the person for the first 24 hours to watch for the warning signs above, while NHS inform mentions up to 72 hours when concussion is only suspected.
pass1.note: Guy's: 24 hours; NHS inform: 72 hours; sources differ

pass1.sentence: Being tired does not mean having to stay awake, say some leaflets, though someone checks on the person overnight.
pass1.note: Leaflet: need not stay awake, someone checks overnight

pass1.sentence: The advice avoids alcohol, recreational drugs, driving and sport.
pass1.note: NHS inform: no driving, alcohol, drugs, sport

pass1.sentence: The usual NHS wording points to a gradual return to normal activity as symptoms settle.
pass1.note: Gradual return; summary of leaflets

pass1.sentence: Mild headache, feeling sick, dizziness, tiredness, poor sleep and trouble concentrating are common after concussion and usually improve within weeks, says NHS inform.
pass1.note: NHS inform: usually improve within weeks

pass1.sentence: Headway calls ongoing symptoms post-concussion syndrome, which it says settles in days or weeks for most people but lasts much longer for some.
pass1.note: Headway: PCS wording

pass1.sentence: Headway advises seeing a GP if symptoms last more than about two weeks, or are severe and not improving.
pass1.note: Headway: GP if more than two weeks

pass1.sentence: Hospital leaflets describe a staged return to work, school and sport, rather than going straight back.
pass1.note: Hospital leaflets: staged return

pass1.sentence: Headway says returning to activity too early can prolong symptoms, and a second head injury before recovery is complete is a serious risk.
pass1.note: Headway: too early can prolong; second injury risk

pass1.sentence: Timings for sport and driving vary between leaflets, so the advice given by the treating team is the one to follow.
pass1.note: Leaflet timings differ
